# Why sleep keeps some memories and lets others go

By a staff writer · 9 min read

For more than a century, psychologists have known that memories fade along a predictable curve. Hermann Ebbinghaus, testing himself on lists of nonsense syllables in the 1880s, found that most of what he learned was gone within a day unless he rehearsed it. What he could not explain was why some traces survive for decades while others vanish by morning. Over the last twenty years, sleep research has begun to supply an answer, and it is less about storage than about selection.

During deep, slow-wave sleep the hippocampus replays patterns of activity that were first laid down while the animal was awake. Recordings in rats running a maze show the same sequence of place cells firing again at night, compressed in time by a factor of ten or more. These replay events are coupled to sleep spindles in the cortex and to slow oscillations that sweep across the brain roughly once a second. When researchers disrupt the coupling, the rats forget the maze; when they strengthen it with gentle sound pulses timed to the slow waves, the rats remember it better.

Replay is not indiscriminate. Experiments in people suggest that the brain favours memories that were tagged as important during learning, either because they were rewarded, because they were emotionally charged, or simply because the learner was told they would be tested later. In one widely cited study, volunteers learned two sets of picture locations and were told that only one set would matter. After a night of sleep they remembered the relevant set far better, even though both had been learned equally well in the evening. Without sleep the advantage disappeared.

This selectivity points to a trade-off rather than a flaw. A system that kept everything would drown in detail and would struggle to generalise. By replaying and strengthening a small fraction of the day's experience, the sleeping brain extracts the regularities that are likely to be useful again and lets the incidental details decay. Neuroscientists sometimes describe this as moving knowledge from a fast, fragile store to a slow, stable one, where it becomes integrated with what was already known.

There is also evidence that forgetting is an active process. Synapses that were strengthened during the day appear to be scaled back during sleep, restoring a balance that keeps neurons responsive to new input. Proteins that erode unused connections are more active in the hours after learning, and blocking them can make animals retain memories they would otherwise lose, including ones they would be better off without.

None of this means that a single night decides the fate of a memory. Recall itself changes the trace: each time a memory is retrieved it becomes briefly malleable and is stored again, sometimes stronger and sometimes altered. The picture that emerges is of memory as a living process in which use, rest and neglect all leave their mark, and in which losing detail is part of how the useful parts are kept.

Researchers are now testing whether the same principles can help people. Timed sound stimulation during sleep is being studied in older adults, whose slow waves weaken with age, and early trials report modest gains in overnight retention.
